# Mercedes-Benz Museum technical tour

Static GitHub Pages site: one page per exhibit showing its mechanism working (three.js), offline after one visit, for
iPhone/iPad Safari (iOS 16.4+, import maps). No bundler: native ES modules; `tools/build.mjs` only stamps the service worker.

## Map
- `index.html` route (lib/app/index.js) · `teaser.html` the three `teaser` stops as scroll stories (lib/app/teaser.js,
  own manifest): each car's stage pins while its steps (intro on the photo, one per component with its cards, background
  with the outline) scroll past and set what it shows · `stop.html?s=<slug>[&r=teaser]` shell for every stop
  (lib/app/shell.js; r=teaser pages among the teaser stops and links back to teaser.html) · `sw.js` offline cache (new root files also go in tools/build.mjs ENTRIES)
- `stops/tour.js` route order, room, level, and `teaser` (slugs): single source for order and prev/next ·
  `stops/<slug>/car.js` pure data (+ photo.jpg)
- `lib/model/` pure maths, Node-tested: linkage (multi-link closure), quarter-car (ride), engine (N-cylinder slider-crank,
  timing, diesel), blower, valvetrain (spring float, desmo), steering (double-pivot trapezoid, centre pivot), differential,
  gearbox (sliding gears), aero (drag, top speed), truss (space frame twist), crash, air-spring (levelling), wankel, cooling,
  belt (two-speed flat-belt drive, hill climbing), hoist (car-transporter deck: cylinder, pulley block, cables), flow (2-D
  lattice-Boltzmann wind tunnel: D2Q9 + Smagorinsky, moving road, drag split)
- `lib/scene/` stage (renderer, cameras, lights, theme tokens, loop), helpers, ghost-body, road, wind-tunnel (CFD view of
  `flow` on the centre plane: speed/pressure/swirl field, body section, smoke streaklines; `--cfd-*` tokens)
- `lib/app/` shell, teaser, viewer (one stop's stage, subsystems, photo view and loop: shared by shell and teaser), panel
  (declarative widgets, API in its header), dom (`h`, `link`), offline, index, theme.css (look after
  mercedes-benz.com: black bar/hero, white page, condensed serif, black photo cards, pills), fonts/ (Instrument Serif, OFL;
  latin + latin-ext for ő/ű), lang.js (head script: saved EN/HU choice or browser language → `<html lang>`), i18n.js
  (`t`, `num`, `loadCar`, `localizePage`), i18n/hu.js (UI catalog keyed by the English text)
- `subsystems/<id>.js` one mechanism each (params documented in each file's header): linkage-suspension, inline-engine,
  roots-blower, desmo-valvetrain, steering, differential, gearbox, radiator, aero, space-frame, crumple-zone,
  air-suspension, wankel, belt-drive, hoist. inline-engine also draws V engines (`leans`: one bank per lean angle,
  opposite cylinders sharing a crankpin)
- `tools/` build, vendor-three, camera (shared pinhole maths), fit-photo-camera (+ photo-fits/*.json), trace-profile
  (+ profile-traces/*.json: side-photo pixels → mm profile), photo-grid (crop + pixel grid + projected profile overlay, PNG
  via Playwright), stop-shot (stage screenshot + fps + page errors; needs `npm run serve`) · `docs/TOUR-POC.md` (model maths §6), `docs/research.md`
- `vendor/three/` is generated by `npm run vendor -- <version>`: never read or edit it.

## Conventions
- Vehicle frame: mm in configs, metres in the scene; x forward, y left, z up; origin per car in `frame.origin`. z = 0 is
  axle height for the first six cars, the ground for the rest: each car.js header says which.
- Camber − = top inboard · toe + = toe-in · travel + = bump · steer + = left.
- Colours only through CSS tokens (`stage.bind`, `stage.tokenMat`, `var(--…)` in SVG): never hard-code theme colours.
  `--band`/`--card` are the fixed-black areas (header bar, index hero, stop cards) and stay dark in both themes.
- Illustrative numbers get a comment in car.js and a line in `unverified` (the page shows it). Sources go in `sources`.
- Panel DOM is built with textContent only; widget ids must be unique within a component.
- English is the source; Hungarian is complete and tested. UI text: `t("English literal", ...args)` with `{0}` placeholders
  (never a variable or template as the key; whole phrases, as Hungarian case endings differ), static HTML: `data-i18n`.
  Logic never compares displayed text: keep English keys/ids and map them to `t(...)` for display. Readout numbers pass
  through `num` (decimal comma). Car text: `stops/<slug>/hu.js`, car.js's shape with only the text fields (list in
  tests/unit/helpers.mjs `TEXT`), null keeps the original; sources and credits stay untranslated.

## Contracts
- car.js: `{ slug, title, name, year, summary, eyebrow, lede, frame?, ride?, orbit?, sun?, body?: { ghost }, photo?,
  components: [{ id, label, subsystem, view: { pos, target }, ghost?: { fill, edge }, params, talk }], note, unverified, sources }`

# Source Document: Mercedes-Benz Museum, Stuttgart - Extended Vehicle & Technology Database

## Overview
This document expands the Mercedes-Benz Museum vehicle database, covering approximately 80% of the prominent, permanent exhibits across the 7 "Legend" rooms and 5 "Collection" rooms. Every entry includes 1-2 noteworthy technological, engineering, or historical highlights, making it an ideal source for NotebookLM data extraction, semantic linking, and study guide generation.

---

## Part 1: The Legend Rooms (Chronological History)

### Legend 1: Pioneers – The Invention of the Automobile (1886–1900)
*   **Daimler Single-Cylinder "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884):** 
    *   First high-speed four-stroke internal combustion engine.
    *   Utilized a hot-tube ignition system, enabling an unprecedented 600 RPM.
*   **Daimler Riding Carriage / Reitwagen (1885):** 
    *   The world's first motorcycle and the first testbed for the Grandfather Clock engine.
    *   Featured a twist-grip style control on the handlebars to apply the brake.
*   **Benz Patent-Motorwagen (1886):** 
    *   The first practical automobile designed from scratch as a car, not a converted carriage.
    *   Featured a lightweight tubular steel frame, wire-spoked wheels, and a trembler coil ignition.
*   **Daimler Motor Carriage (1886):** 
    *   The world’s first four-wheeled automobile.
    *   Literally a horse-drawn carriage purchased by Daimler and retrofitted with a 1.1 hp engine.
*   **Benz Victoria (1893):** 
    *   First Benz with double-pivot (kingpin) steering, solving the stability issues of earlier single-pivot designs.
*   **Benz Motor Velocipede "Velo" (1894):** 
    *   Considered the world's first large-scale production car (over 1,200 units built).
    *   Weighed only 280 kg, achieving a top speed of 20 km/h.
*   **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** 
    *   Introduced the tubular radiator (designed by Wilhelm Maybach), vastly improving engine cooling for heavy payloads.

### Legend 2: Birth of the Brand (1900–1914)
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 40 PS (1902):** 
    *   Introduced the modern automobile layout: a low center of gravity, front-mounted engine, and a honeycomb radiator.
    *   The honeycomb radiator was a monumental leap in cooling efficiency, drastically reducing the amount of water needed.
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 60 PS (1903):** 
    *   Featured overhead intake valves and a massive 9.2-liter four-cylinder engine.
    *   Capable of reaching speeds over 100 km/h, making it a dominating force in early motorsport.
*   **Milnes-Daimler Double-Decker Bus (1904):** 
    *   Early application of a robust internal combustion engine in mass transit.
    *   Featured solid rubber tires and a chain drive to the rear wheels.

### Legend 3: Times of Change (1914–1945)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928):** 
    *   "SSK" stands for Super Sport Kurz (Short). Its shortened wheelbase made it incredibly agile for hillclimbs.
    *   Powered by a 7.1-liter supercharged engine where the Roots blower engaged only when the throttle was fully depressed.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 770 "Grosser Mercedes" (1930):**

# Source Document: Mercedes-Benz Museum, Stuttgart - Vehicle & Exhibit Database

## Part 1: Comprehensive List of Displayed Cars (Highlights)
The Mercedes-Benz Museum spans nine floors and 16,500 square meters, housing a total of 160 vehicles and over 1,500 exhibits. While a complete manifest of all 160 vehicles is subject to rotation, the permanent exhibition is structured into 7 chronological "Legend Rooms" and 5 thematic "Collection Rooms". Below is the comprehensive list of the most prominent vehicles on display, organized by their respective exhibit areas:

### Legend 1: Pioneers – The Invention of the Automobile (1886–1900)
*   **Daimler Single-Cylinder "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884):** A structural sculpture of steel and brass that heralded modern mobility.
*   **Daimler Riding Carriage / Reitwagen (1885):** The world's first motorcycle.
*   **Benz Patent-Motorwagen (1886):** Recognized as the first functional car powered by a combustion engine.
*   **Daimler Motorboat "Marie" (1888):** A prominent early application of the combustion engine for water travel. 
*   **Benz Victoria (1893):** An early endurance vehicle that tackled a 939-kilometer journey.
*   **Benz Motor Velocipede (1894):** Regarded as the first large-scale production car.
*   **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** An early commercial truck capable of a 500 kg payload.

### Legend 2 & 3: Birth of the Brand & Times of Change (1900–1945)
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 40 PS (1902):** Often referred to as the oldest Mercedes still in existence and the first automobile of the modern age.
*   **Milnes-Daimler Double-Decker Bus (1904):** An early transit vehicle used in London.
*   **Benz 200 PS "Lightning Benz" / "Blitzen Benz" (1909):** A massive 1,312 cu in displacement racer capable of 141 mph.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928):** A legendary pre-war open-wheel sports car with an angled front grille.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 540 K Streamliner (1938):** A masterclass in pre-war aerodynamic aesthetics.
*   **Mercedes-Benz L6500 Pritschenwagen (1938):** A heavy-duty pre-war industrial cargo truck.

### Legend 4 & 5: Post-war Miracle & Visionaries (1945–1982)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SL "Gullwing" (1954):** The iconic dream car of the 1950s with upward-opening doors.
*   **Mercedes-Benz Rennwagen-Schnelltransporter "Blue Wonder" (1955):** A high-speed flat-bed transport truck for race cars.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe (1955):** A brutally fast roadster built from race car mechanics.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 SL (1955):** A beautiful classic roadster.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 220 S "Tailfin" (1959):** Known for its North American-inspired rear directional wings.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.3 (1968):** The top-of-the-line luxury predecessor to the modern S-Class.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 230 G "Papamobil" (1980):** The iconic modified G-Wagen used by Pope John Paul II.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 500 SLC Rallyewagen (1980):** A rare long-distance rally racer.

### Legend 6, Legend 7 & Collection Rooms
*   **Mercedes-Benz Vision R 320 CDI (2005):** A concept vehicle showcasing emission-free mobility ambitions.
*   **Mercedes-Maybach 6 Concept:** A modern, dramatic luxury showcase.
*   **Mercedes-Benz C 111-II:** An experimental concept car.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 1624 Car Transporter:** A massive multi-level commercial vehicle transporter positioned high up in Collection Room 2.
*   **Silver Arrows Racing Cars:** Found in Legend 7 on an expansive banked curve display, celebrating the brand's racing lineage.

---

## Part 2: Vehicles Exhibited for "Close-Up" Inspection
The museum has a specifically curated "Close-up" series, which highlights specific exhibits that allow visitors to see mechanical elements, raw craftsmanship, and intricate detailing at close range. These exhibits are specifically designed to expose their inner workings:

1.  **Daimler Riding Carriage (1885):** Visitors can view the exposed two simple control levers (a metal handle for mixture formation and a wooden knob for the block brake), the glow-tube ignition tank, and the leather drive belts.
2.  **Daimler 'Grandfather Clock' Engine (1884):** Displayed as a bare steel and brass sculpture so the vertical cylinder and round crankcase can be closely examined.
3.  **Benz Victoria (1893):** Positioned so the mechanical geometry of its early kingpin steering linkage can be seen.
4.  **Daimler Motorboat 'Marie' (1888):** Visitors can inspect the white-painted doors that discreetly concealed the single-cylinder engine from passengers.
5.  **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** The sieve-like front panel is exposed to show the tubular radiator designed by Wilhelm Maybach.
6.  **Mercedes-Benz 1624 Car Transporter:** Exhibited so the heavy-duty hydraulic control elements and the hybrid drive of the loading platforms (pulley blocks and hydraulics) can be inspected in high detail.

---

## Part 3: Technical Highlights & Corresponding Cars (Worthy of Separate Discussion)
This structured list isolates the most important technical innovations present at the museum. It maps directly to specific vehicles and serves as an excellent foundation for a NotebookLM study guide, visual presentation, or isolated audio discussion.

*   **First High-Speed Four-Stroke Engine**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle/Exhibit:** Daimler "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884)
    *   **Technical Details:** Developed in a garden house by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach. Initially produced 1 hp (0.5 hp in the riding carriage) at a then-astounding 600 revolutions per minute.
*   **Kingpin Steering Innovation**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Benz Victoria (1893)
    *   **Technical Details:** Replaced crude central-pivot steering systems, making cornering noticeably safer and allowing vehicles to comfortably navigate nearly 1,000 km journeys on primitive roads.
*   **Invention of the Tubular Radiator**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899)
    *   **Technical Details:** Created by Wilhelm Maybach to drastically improve engine cooling efficiency under loads, which enabled commercial vehicles to securely carry payloads up to 500 kg at 16 km/h.
*   **Supercharged Hillclimb Engineering**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928)
    *   **Technical Details:** Featured a massive 220-hp supercharged inline-six engine housed in a skinny, lightweight fuselage built specifically for dominance in uphill racing.
*   **Early Implementation of Modern Aerodynamics**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 540 K Streamliner (1938)
    *   **Technical Details:** Despite featuring free-standing front mudguards, it utilized sweeping, wind-tunnel-tested curves to achieve a highly impressive drag coefficient (Cd) of just 0.36. 
*   **High-Torque Heavy Diesel Powertrain**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz L6500 Pritschenwagen (1938)
    *   **Technical Details:** Equipped with a whopping 12.5-liter six-cylinder diesel engine positioned in front of the forward axle, enabling the transport of up to 14,000 pounds of payload.
*   **Bridging Race-Car Physics with Road-Car Usability**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe (1955)
    *   **Technical Details:** Housed the mechanical chassis and a 3.0-liter inline-eight engine (310 hp) from a pure race car. Capable of an astonishing 180 mph in an era where most passenger cars struggled to hit 100 mph.
*   **High-Speed Commercial Aerodynamics**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz Rennwagen-Schnelltransporter (1955)
    *   **Technical Details:** A heavy transport flat-bed utilizing a slippery aerodynamic profile and a 3.0-liter inline-six engine (approx. 200 hp), enabling a loaded truck to cruise on the Autobahn at 106 mph.

# Source Document: Mercedes-Benz Museum, Stuttgart - Vehicle & Exhibit Database

## Part 1: Comprehensive List of Displayed Cars (Highlights)
The Mercedes-Benz Museum spans nine floors and 16,500 square meters, housing a total of 160 vehicles and over 1,500 exhibits. While a complete manifest of all 160 vehicles is subject to rotation, the permanent exhibition is structured into 7 chronological "Legend Rooms" and 5 thematic "Collection Rooms". Below is the comprehensive list of the most prominent vehicles on display, organized by their respective exhibit areas:

### Legend 1: Pioneers – The Invention of the Automobile (1886–1900)
*   **Daimler Single-Cylinder "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884):** A structural sculpture of steel and brass that heralded modern mobility.
*   **Daimler Riding Carriage / Reitwagen (1885):** The world's first motorcycle.
*   **Benz Patent-Motorwagen (1886):** Recognized as the first functional car powered by a combustion engine.
*   **Daimler Motorboat "Marie" (1888):** A prominent early application of the combustion engine for water travel. 
*   **Benz Victoria (1893):** An early endurance vehicle that tackled a 939-kilometer journey.
*   **Benz Motor Velocipede (1894):** Regarded as the first large-scale production car.
*   **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** An early commercial truck capable of a 500 kg payload.

### Legend 2 & 3: Birth of the Brand & Times of Change (1900–1945)
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 40 PS (1902):** Often referred to as the oldest Mercedes still in existence and the first automobile of the modern age.
*   **Milnes-Daimler Double-Decker Bus (1904):** An early transit vehicle used in London.
*   **Benz 200 PS "Lightning Benz" / "Blitzen Benz" (1909):** A massive 1,312 cu in displacement racer capable of 141 mph.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928):** A legendary pre-war open-wheel sports car with an angled front grille.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 540 K Streamliner (1938):** A masterclass in pre-war aerodynamic aesthetics.
*   **Mercedes-Benz L6500 Pritschenwagen (1938):** A heavy-duty pre-war industrial cargo truck.

### Legend 4 & 5: Post-war Miracle & Visionaries (1945–1982)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SL "Gullwing" (1954):** The iconic dream car of the 1950s with upward-opening doors.
*   **Mercedes-Benz Rennwagen-Schnelltransporter "Blue Wonder" (1955):** A high-speed flat-bed transport truck for race cars.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe (1955):** A brutally fast roadster built from race car mechanics.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 SL (1955):** A beautiful classic roadster.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 220 S "Tailfin" (1959):** Known for its North American-inspired rear directional wings.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.3 (1968):** The top-of-the-line luxury predecessor to the modern S-Class.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 230 G "Papamobil" (1980):** The iconic modified G-Wagen used by Pope John Paul II.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 500 SLC Rallyewagen (1980):** A rare long-distance rally racer.

### Legend 6, Legend 7 & Collection Rooms
*   **Mercedes-Benz Vision R 320 CDI (2005):** A concept vehicle showcasing emission-free mobility ambitions.
*   **Mercedes-Maybach 6 Concept:** A modern, dramatic luxury showcase.
*   **Mercedes-Benz C 111-II:** An experimental concept car.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 1624 Car Transporter:** A massive multi-level commercial vehicle transporter positioned high up in Collection Room 2.
*   **Silver Arrows Racing Cars:** Found in Legend 7 on an expansive banked curve display, celebrating the brand's racing lineage.

---

## Part 2: Vehicles Exhibited for "Close-Up" Inspection
The museum has a specifically curated "Close-up" series, which highlights specific exhibits that allow visitors to see mechanical elements, raw craftsmanship, and intricate detailing at close range. These exhibits are specifically designed to expose their inner workings:

1.  **Daimler Riding Carriage (1885):** Visitors can view the exposed two simple control levers (a metal handle for mixture formation and a wooden knob for the block brake), the glow-tube ignition tank, and the leather drive belts.
2.  **Daimler 'Grandfather Clock' Engine (1884):** Displayed as a bare steel and brass sculpture so the vertical cylinder and round crankcase can be closely examined.
3.  **Benz Victoria (1893):** Positioned so the mechanical geometry of its early kingpin steering linkage can be seen.
4.  **Daimler Motorboat 'Marie' (1888):** Visitors can inspect the white-painted doors that discreetly concealed the single-cylinder engine from passengers.
5.  **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** The sieve-like front panel is exposed to show the tubular radiator designed by Wilhelm Maybach.
6.  **Mercedes-Benz 1624 Car Transporter:** Exhibited so the heavy-duty hydraulic control elements and the hybrid drive of the loading platforms (pulley blocks and hydraulics) can be inspected in high detail.

---

## Part 3: Technical Highlights & Corresponding Cars (Worthy of Separate Discussion)
This structured list isolates the most important technical innovations present at the museum. It maps directly to specific vehicles and serves as an excellent foundation for a NotebookLM study guide, visual presentation, or isolated audio discussion.

*   **First High-Speed Four-Stroke Engine**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle/Exhibit:** Daimler "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884)
    *   **Technical Details:** Developed in a garden house by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach. Initially produced 1 hp (0.5 hp in the riding carriage) at a then-astounding 600 revolutions per minute.
*   **Kingpin Steering Innovation**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Benz Victoria (1893)
    *   **Technical Details:** Replaced crude central-pivot steering systems, making cornering noticeably safer and allowing vehicles to comfortably navigate nearly 1,000 km journeys on primitive roads.
*   **Invention of the Tubular Radiator**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899)
    *   **Technical Details:** Created by Wilhelm Maybach to drastically improve engine cooling efficiency under loads, which enabled commercial vehicles to securely carry payloads up to 500 kg at 16 km/h.
*   **Supercharged Hillclimb Engineering**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928)
    *   **Technical Details:** Featured a massive 220-hp supercharged inline-six engine housed in a skinny, lightweight fuselage built specifically for dominance in uphill racing.
*   **Early Implementation of Modern Aerodynamics**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 540 K Streamliner (1938)
    *   **Technical Details:** Despite featuring free-standing front mudguards, it utilized sweeping, wind-tunnel-tested curves to achieve a highly impressive drag coefficient (Cd) of just 0.36. 
*   **High-Torque Heavy Diesel Powertrain**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz L6500 Pritschenwagen (1938)
    *   **Technical Details:** Equipped with a whopping 12.5-liter six-cylinder diesel engine positioned in front of the forward axle, enabling the transport of up to 14,000 pounds of payload.
*   **Bridging Race-Car Physics with Road-Car Usability**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe (1955)
    *   **Technical Details:** Housed the mechanical chassis and a 3.0-liter inline-eight engine (310 hp) from a pure race car. Capable of an astonishing 180 mph in an era where most passenger cars struggled to hit 100 mph.
*   **High-Speed Commercial Aerodynamics**
    *   **Corresponding Vehicle:** Mercedes-Benz Rennwagen-Schnelltransporter (1955)
    *   **Technical Details:** A heavy transport flat-bed utilizing a slippery aerodynamic profile and a 3.0-liter inline-six engine (approx. 200 hp), enabling a loaded truck to cruise on the Autobahn at 106 mph.

mkdir -p /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kunabel-workspace-MercedesExperience/9e81937d-309b-4c6b-b1d5-aba6e1a64c2b/scratchpad/tools && cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kunabel-workspace-MercedesExperience/9e81937d-309b-4c6b-b1d5-aba6e1a64c2b/scratchpad/tools/cs.py <<'EOF'
# Commons search: python3 -I cs.py "query" [n]  -> title, size, license, author
import sys, json, urllib.request, urllib.parse, re
q = sys.argv[1]; n = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 15
UA = {"User-Agent": "museum-tour-photo-search/1.0 (research script)"}
def get(params):
    url = "https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({**params, "format": "json"})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA)))
r = get({"action": "query", "generator": "search", "gsrsearch": q, "gsrnamespace": 6, "gsrlimit": n,
         "prop": "imageinfo", "iiprop": "size|extmetadata|url", "iiextmetadatafilter": "LicenseShortName|Artist"})
for p in sorted(r.get("query", {}).get("pages", {}).values(), key=lambda p: p.get("index", 0)):
    ii = p["imageinfo"][0]; md = ii.get("extmetadata", {})
    art = re.sub("<[^>]+>", "", md.get("Artist", {}).get("value", ""))[:40]
    print(f'{ii["width"]}x{ii["height"]} | {md.get("LicenseShortName", {}).get("value", "?")} | {art} | {p["title"][5:]}')
EOF

+// Four-wheel drive through three differentials: front, centre and rear, each open or locked. With traction control by the
+// brakes (4ETS, brake > 0) a wheel that would spin on an open differential is braked instead, so its side of the
+// differential can pass on up to `brake` more. Forces at the tyres in N, wheels ordered fl, fr, rl, rr.
+// p = { force (N: the engine's drive at the wheels, all four together), normal (N per wheel), mu: [4], front, centre,
+//   rear (true = locked), brake (N a wheel brake can hold back, 0 = none), resist (N needed to move the car) }.
+export function traction4({ force, normal, mu, front, centre, rear, brake = 0, resist = 0 }) {
+  // One axle: input = the force put into its differential; drive = what its tyres push. Open, each side takes input/2,
+  // which may be up to its grip plus what its brake can hold; locked, the sides share it in proportion to grip.

2. Key Technical Concepts:

   Platform and site structure:
   - Static GitHub Pages site for iOS 16.4+ Safari: native ES modules plus import maps, three.js in vendor/three (never read or edit it), no bundler.
   - tools/build.mjs stamps sw.js for offline caching; new root files go in its ENTRIES.
   - stops/tour.js is the single source for route order, room, level and `teaser`.
   - Each stop is pure data: stops/<slug>/car.js, photo.jpg and hu.js.

   car.js contract:

   - API: `create(ctx = { stage, carRoot, frame, ride, panel, reducedMotion, t }, params)` returns `{ layout({ active, onPhoto }), update(dt, { onPhoto }) }`.
   - Panel widgets are declarative: readouts, buttons (toggle/pressed), slider, svg, legend, key, text, list, cells, meter, trace.
   - Colours only through tokens: `stage.tokenMat("--l1")` and `stage.bind`.

   ```js
   import { t } from "./i18n.js";

   import { stageElement, mountViewer, caveats } from "./viewer.js";
   const step = (state, ...kids) => ({ state, el: h("section", { class: "step" }, kids) });
   export function story(car, { title = "h2", more = null } = {}) {
     const first = car.components[0].id;
     const comps = car.components.map(c => step({ comp: c.id, view: "model", outline: false }, h("h3", {}, c.label)));
     const steps = [
       step({ comp: first, view: "photo", outline: false }, h("div", { class: "eyebrow" }, car.eyebrow), h(title, {}, car.title), h("p", { class: "lede" }, car.lede)),
       ...comps,
       step({ comp: first, view: "photo", outline: true }, h("footer", {}, h("h3", {}, t("Background")),
         h("p", {}, t("Back on the museum photo: the mechanism where it sits, inside the car's outline.")),
         car.note ? h("p", {}, car.note) : null, ...caveats(car), more)),
     ];
     steps[0].el.classList.add("on");
     const stageEl = stageElement(car);
     const el = h("article", { class: "story", "aria-label": car.name }, h("div", { class: "story-stage" }, stageEl), h("div", { class: "steps" }, steps.map(s => s.el)));
     return { car, el, stageEl, steps, comps, at: 0, viewer: null };

       frames: () => s.viewer?.stage.stats.frames ?? 0, triangles: () => s.viewer?.stage.renderer.info.render.triangles ?? 0 }));
   }
   ```

3	// Cornering: each driven wheel follows its own circle about the turn centre, so the outer wheel turns faster.

6	export function cornerSpeeds({ halfTrack, wheelR }, radius, v) {

8	  const left = v * (1 - k) / wheelR, right = v * (1 + k) / wheelR;
9	  return { left, right, carrier: (left + right) / 2, diff: (right - left) / 2 };

13	// Locked: the axle turns as one shaft and each wheel can push up to its own grip.

15	export function traction({ torque, wheelR, normal, muL, muR, locked, resist = 0 }) {
16	  const gripL = muL * normal, gripR = muR * normal, want = torque / wheelR;
17	  let fL, fR, spinL, spinR;
18	  if (locked) {
19	    const grip = gripL + gripR, f = Math.min(want, grip);
20	    fL = grip ? f * gripL / grip : 0; fR = f - fL;
21	    spinL = spinR = want > grip;
22	  } else {
23	    // The wheel with less grip spins first; that caps the torque on both sides, so the other wheel never spins.
24	    const each = Math.min(want / 2, gripL, gripR);

34	// differential can pass on up to `brake` more. Forces at the tyres in N, wheels ordered fl, fr, rl, rr.
35	// p = { force (N: the engine's drive at the wheels, all four together), normal (N per wheel), mu: [4], front, centre,
36	//   rear (true = locked), brake (N a wheel brake can hold back, 0 = none), resist (N needed to move the car) }.

# Download a Commons file at 1200 px wide: python3 -I dl.py outdir slug "File title" [width]
import sys, json, urllib.request, urllib.parse, time
out, slug, title = sys.argv[1:4]; w = int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 1200
UA = {"User-Agent": "museum-tour-photo-search/1.0 (research script)"}
url = "https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"action": "query", "titles": "File:" + title, "prop": "imageinfo", "iiprop": "url|size", "iiurlwidth": w, "format": "json"})
p = next(iter(json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA)))["query"]["pages"].values()))
ii = p["imageinfo"][0]; src = ii["thumburl"] if ii["width"] > w else ii["url"]
data = None
for k in range(6):
    try:
        data = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(src, headers=UA)).read(); break
    except Exception as e: print("retry", e); time.sleep(15 * (k + 1))
if data is None: raise SystemExit(f"failed {slug}")
open(f"{out}/{slug}.jpg", "wb").write(data); print(slug, len(data), ii["descriptionurl"] if "descriptionurl" in ii else "")

lines: +// Permanent four-wheel drive through three differentials, from above (lib/model/differential.js traction4). Open, each
+// differential sends equal torque both ways, so a single wheel on ice caps the drive of everything behind it. The G-Class

# Source Document: Mercedes-Benz Museum, Stuttgart - Extended Vehicle & Technology Database

## Overview
This document expands the Mercedes-Benz Museum vehicle database, covering approximately 80% of the prominent, permanent exhibits across the 7 "Legend" rooms and 5 "Collection" rooms. Every entry includes 1-2 noteworthy technological, engineering, or historical highlights, making it an ideal source for NotebookLM data extraction, semantic linking, and study guide generation.

---

## Part 1: The Legend Rooms (Chronological History)

### Legend 1: Pioneers – The Invention of the Automobile (1886–1900)
*   **Daimler Single-Cylinder "Grandfather Clock" Engine (1884):** 
    *   First high-speed four-stroke internal combustion engine.
    *   Utilized a hot-tube ignition system, enabling an unprecedented 600 RPM.
*   **Daimler Riding Carriage / Reitwagen (1885):** 
    *   The world's first motorcycle and the first testbed for the Grandfather Clock engine.
    *   Featured a twist-grip style control on the handlebars to apply the brake.
*   **Benz Patent-Motorwagen (1886):** 
    *   The first practical automobile designed from scratch as a car, not a converted carriage.
    *   Featured a lightweight tubular steel frame, wire-spoked wheels, and a trembler coil ignition.
*   **Daimler Motor Carriage (1886):** 
    *   The world’s first four-wheeled automobile.
    *   Literally a horse-drawn carriage purchased by Daimler and retrofitted with a 1.1 hp engine.
*   **Benz Victoria (1893):** 
    *   First Benz with double-pivot (kingpin) steering, solving the stability issues of earlier single-pivot designs.
*   **Benz Motor Velocipede "Velo" (1894):** 
    *   Considered the world's first large-scale production car (over 1,200 units built).
    *   Weighed only 280 kg, achieving a top speed of 20 km/h.
*   **Daimler Motorised Business Vehicle (1899):** 
    *   Introduced the tubular radiator (designed by Wilhelm Maybach), vastly improving engine cooling for heavy payloads.

### Legend 2: Birth of the Brand (1900–1914)
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 40 PS (1902):** 
    *   Introduced the modern automobile layout: a low center of gravity, front-mounted engine, and a honeycomb radiator.
    *   The honeycomb radiator was a monumental leap in cooling efficiency, drastically reducing the amount of water needed.
*   **Mercedes-Simplex 60 PS (1903):** 
    *   Featured overhead intake valves and a massive 9.2-liter four-cylinder engine.
    *   Capable of reaching speeds over 100 km/h, making it a dominating force in early motorsport.
*   **Milnes-Daimler Double-Decker Bus (1904):** 
    *   Early application of a robust internal combustion engine in mass transit.
    *   Featured solid rubber tires and a chain drive to the rear wheels.

### Legend 3: Times of Change (1914–1945)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 27/170 Typ SSK (1928):** 
    *   "SSK" stands for Super Sport Kurz (Short). Its shortened wheelbase made it incredibly agile for hillclimbs.
    *   Powered by a 7.1-liter supercharged engine where the Roots blower engaged only when the throttle was fully depressed.

*   **Mercedes-Benz 770 "Grosser Mercedes" (1930):** 
    *   A massive luxury vehicle featuring an inline-eight engine with dual ignition (two spark plugs per cylinder: one magneto, one battery-powered) for ultimate reliability.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 500 K / 540 K Spezial-Roadster (1934–1939):** 
    *   Featured independent suspension on all four wheels (double wishbones in front, swing axles in rear) for exceptional ride comfort.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 260 D (1936):** 
    *   The world’s first series-production diesel passenger car.
    *   Utilized a pre-chamber fuel injection system for smoother combustion and high fuel economy, making it an instant favorite for taxi fleets.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 540 K Streamliner (1938):** 
    *   Pioneered wind-tunnel-optimized aluminum bodywork, achieving a drag coefficient of 0.36.

### Legend 4: Post-war Miracle (1945–1960)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 "Adenauer" (1951):** 
    *   The flagship post-war luxury sedan, featuring an electrically operated torsion bar suspension system on the rear axle to handle heavy loads without sagging.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SL "Gullwing" (1954):** 
    *   The first production car to feature direct fuel injection (adapted from aviation technology).
    *   Its iconic doors were born from necessity: a rigid, lightweight tubular spaceframe ran high along the sides, preventing standard doors from being fitted.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 220 "Ponton" (1954):** 
    *   The first Mercedes-Benz passenger car with a self-supporting, unitized body structure (monocoque), improving crash safety and saving weight.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 SL (1955):** 
    *   Pioneered the concept of a "lifestyle" roadster, utilizing the shortened monocoque platform of the "Ponton" sedan rather than a complex spaceframe.

### Legend 5: Visionaries & Safety (1960–1982)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 230 SL "Pagoda" (1963):** 
    *   The world's first sports car designed with a rigid passenger safety cell and front/rear crumple zones (invented by Béla Barényi).
    *   Its concave "pagoda" hardtop design allowed for larger windows and greater structural rigidity.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 600 "Pullman" (1963):** 
    *   Featured a highly complex 150-bar "comfort hydraulic" system that silently powered the windows, seats, sunroof, and automated closing doors.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.3 (1968):** 
    *   The original "super sedan": Mercedes engineers secretly dropped the massive 6.3-liter V8 from the 600 limousine into the smaller W109 body.
    *   Featured advanced self-leveling air suspension.
*   **Mercedes-Benz C 111 Experimental Series (1969–1979):** 
    *   A bright orange testbed for Wankel rotary engines and aerodynamic fiberglass bodywork.
    *   Later versions (C 111-IID, III) tested record-breaking turbodiesel engines to prove diesel could be fast.
*   **Mercedes-Benz ESF 22 Experimental Safety Vehicle (1973):** 
    *   Showcased pioneering safety tech years before production, including driver airbags, seatbelt tensioners, and anti-lock brakes (ABS).

### Legend 6: New Start (1982–Present)
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 E (W 201) "Baby Benz" (1982):** 
    *   Introduced the revolutionary 5-link independent rear suspension, which decoupled wheel movements to provide unprecedented grip and ride quality.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 500 SL (R 129) (1989):** 
    *   Featured an automatic pop-up roll bar that deployed in just 0.3 seconds if sensors detected an impending rollover.
*   **Mercedes-Benz A-Class (W 168) (1997):** 
    *   Pioneered the "sandwich floor" concept: in a severe frontal impact, the engine and transmission slide underneath the passenger floor rather than intruding into the cabin.
*   **Mercedes-Benz SLK (R 170) (1996):** 
    *   The first modern production car to feature a fully automatic, retractable electro-hydraulic steel hardtop (Vario-roof).
*   **Mercedes-Benz SLS AMG (2010):** 
    *   The first vehicle designed entirely in-house by AMG. 
    *   Since it used gullwing doors, it featured explosive bolts in the door hinges that would detonate to allow occupants to escape in the event of a rollover crash.

### Legend 7: Silver Arrows - Races & Records
*   **Benz 200 PS "Lightning Benz" / "Blitzen Benz" (1909):** 
    *   Powered by a monstrous 21.5-liter four-cylinder engine. 
    *   Broke the 200 km/h barrier, making it faster than any airplane or train of its era.
*   **Mercedes-Benz W 25 (1934):** 
    *   The origin of the "Silver Arrow" legend. Engineers allegedly scraped off the white lead-based paint down to bare aluminum overnight to meet the strict 750 kg maximum weight limit.
*   **Mercedes-Benz W 196 R (1954):** 
    *   Used desmodromic valve gear (valves opened and closed positively by cams, rather than closed by springs), preventing valve float at ultra-high RPMs.
    *   Exhibited in both open-wheel and aerodynamic "Streamliner" body styles.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR (W 196 S) (1955):** 
    *   An evolution of the Formula 1 car for endurance racing. 
    *   Featured an air brake—a massive flap behind the driver that flipped up to dramatically increase drag and assist braking from high speeds.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II (1990):** 
    *   A highly sought-after DTM homologation special. 
    *   Its radical, wind-tunnel-optimized body kit reduced lift completely and achieved a remarkably low drag coefficient despite its massive rear wing.

---

## Part 2: Highlights from the Collection Rooms

### Gallery of Voyagers & Carriers (Commercial & Mass Transit)
*   **Mercedes-Benz LO 1112 Bus (1969):** 
    *   A brightly colored South American "Colectivo" bus from Buenos Aires, showing how the reliable short-nose truck chassis was adapted for global passenger transport.
*   **Mercedes-Benz LP 333 "Millipede" Truck (1958):** 
    *   Featured two steered front axles. This unique twin-steering layout was an engineering workaround to comply with strict 1950s German laws regarding maximum axle loads.
*   **Mercedes-Benz O 302 Coach (1974):** 
    *   Used as the official team bus during the 1974 FIFA World Cup. Showcased early adoption of standard roof-mounted air conditioning units for passenger comfort.

### Gallery of Helpers (Emergency & Utility)
*   **Unimog (Universal-Motor-Gerät):** 
    *   Utilizes portal axles (the axle tube is above the center of the wheel hub) for massive ground clearance.
    *   The chassis ladder frame is specifically designed to flex, acting as a part of the suspension system during extreme off-roading.
*   **Mercedes-Benz G-Class (Various Years):** 
    *   Features three fully lockable differentials (front, center, and rear) operable while driving, making it nearly unstoppable in low-traction environments.

### Gallery of Celebrities & Heroes
*   **Mercedes-Benz 230 G "Papamobil" (1980):** 
    *   Built for Pope John Paul II. The elevated transparent cupola was originally just weather protection but was later upgraded to bulletproof polycarbonate following the 1981 assassination attempt.
*   **Mercedes-Benz ML 320 "Jurassic Park" Edition (1997):** 
    *   Showcased the launch of the M-Class (W 163), which featured an electronic traction system (4ETS) that simulated locking differentials by braking spinning wheels, a major leap for luxury SUVs at the time.
*   **Princess Diana’s Mercedes-Benz 500 SL (1991):** 
    *   Represented a shift in British royal tradition (being a foreign car) and showcased the top-tier luxury and safety (pop-up roll bar) of the R 129 generation.

*   **Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR (W 196 S) (1955):** 
    *   An evolution of the Formula 1 car for endurance racing. 
    *   Featured an air brake—a massive flap behind the driver that flipped up to dramatically increase drag and assist braking from high speeds.
*   **Mercedes-Benz 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II (1990):** 
    *   A highly sought-after DTM homologation special. 
    *   Its radical, wind-tunnel-optimized body kit reduced lift completely and achieved a remarkably low drag coefficient despite its massive rear wing.

---

## Part 2: Highlights from the Collection Rooms

### Gallery of Voyagers & Carriers (Commercial & Mass Transit)
*   **Mercedes-Benz LO 1112 Bus (1969):** 
    *   A brightly colored South American "Colectivo" bus from Buenos Aires, showing how the reliable short-nose truck chassis was adapted for global passenger transport.
*   **Mercedes-Benz LP 333 "Millipede" Truck (1958):** 
    *   Featured two steered front axles. This unique twin-steering layout was an engineering workaround to comply with strict 1950s German laws regarding maximum axle loads.
*   **Mercedes-Benz O 302 Coach (1974):** 
    *   Used as the official team bus during the 1974 FIFA World Cup. Showcased early adoption of standard roof-mounted air conditioning units for passenger comfort.

### Gallery of Helpers (Emergency & Utility)
*   **Unimog (Universal-Motor-Gerät):** 
    *   Utilizes portal axles (the axle tube is above the center of the wheel hub) for massive ground clearance.
    *   The chassis ladder frame is specifically designed to flex, acting as a part of the suspension system during extreme off-roading.
*   **Mercedes-Benz G-Class (Various Years):** 
    *   Features three fully lockable differentials (front, center, and rear) operable while driving, making it nearly unstoppable in low-traction environments.

### Gallery of Celebrities & Heroes
*   **Mercedes-Benz 230 G "Papamobil" (1980):** 
    *   Built for Pope John Paul II. The elevated transparent cupola was originally just weather protection but was later upgraded to bulletproof polycarbonate following the 1981 assassination attempt.
*   **Mercedes-Benz ML 320 "Jurassic Park" Edition (1997):** 
    *   Showcased the launch of the M-Class (W 163), which featured an electronic traction system (4ETS) that simulated locking differentials by braking spinning wheels, a major leap for luxury SUVs at the time.
*   **Princess Diana’s Mercedes-Benz 500 SL (1991):** 
    *   Represented a shift in British royal tradition (being a foreign car) and showcased the top-tier luxury and safety (pop-up roll bar) of the R 129 generation.

# Fetch Commons photos gently: python3 -I fetch.py outdir list.txt (lines "slug|File title"). Writes <slug>.jpg and meta.json.
import sys, json, time, urllib.request, urllib.parse, re
out, lst = sys.argv[1:3]
UA = {"User-Agent": "museum-tour-photo-search/1.0 (research script)"}
get = u => urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(u, headers=UA), timeout=60).read()
meta = {}
try: meta = json.load(open(f"{out}/meta.json"))
except Exception: pass
for line in open(lst):
    slug, title = line.strip().split("|", 1)
    if slug in meta: continue
    q = "https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"action": "query", "titles": "File:" + title, "prop": "imageinfo", "iiprop": "url|size|extmetadata", "iiurlwidth": 1280, "format": "json"})
    ii = next(iter(json.loads(get(q))["query"]["pages"].values()))["imageinfo"][0]
    src = ii["url"] if ii["width"] <= 1600 else ii["thumburl"]
    for k in range(4):
        try: data = get(src); break
        except Exception as e: print(slug, "retry", str(e)[:60], flush=True); data = None; time.sleep(60 * (k + 1))
    if not data: print(slug, "FAILED", flush=True); continue
    open(f"{out}/{slug}.jpg", "wb").write(data)
    em = ii.get("extmetadata", {}); clean = lambda k: re.sub("<[^>]+>", "", em.get(k, {}).get("value", "")).strip()
    meta[slug] = {"title": title, "w": ii["width"], "h": ii["height"], "author": clean("Artist"), "license": clean("LicenseShortName"), "url": ii["descriptionurl"]}
    json.dump(meta, open(f"{out}/meta.json", "w"), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
    print(slug, len(data), meta[slug]["license"], meta[slug]["author"], flush=True)
    time.sleep(25)
EOF

# Fetch Commons photos gently: python3 -I fetch.py outdir list.txt (lines "slug|File title"). Writes <slug>.jpg and meta.json.
import sys, json, time, urllib.request, urllib.parse, re
out, lst = sys.argv[1:3]
UA = {"User-Agent": "museum-tour-photo-search/1.0 (research script)"}
get = u => urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(u, headers=UA), timeout=60).read()
meta = {}
try: meta = json.load(open(f"{out}/meta.json"))
except Exception: pass
for line in open(lst):
    slug, title = line.strip().split("|", 1)
    if slug in meta: continue
    q = "https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"action": "query", "titles": "File:" + title, "prop": "imageinfo", "iiprop": "url|size|extmetadata", "iiurlwidth": 1280, "format": "json"})
    ii = next(iter(json.loads(get(q))["query"]["pages"].values()))["imageinfo"][0]
    src = ii["url"] if ii["width"] <= 1600 else ii["thumburl"]
    for k in range(4):
        try: data = get(src); break
        except Exception as e: print(slug, "retry", str(e)[:60], flush=True); data = None; time.sleep(60 * (k + 1))
    if not data: print(slug, "FAILED", flush=True); continue
    open(f"{out}/{slug}.jpg", "wb").write(data)
    em = ii.get("extmetadata", {}); clean = lambda k: re.sub("<[^>]+>", "", em.get(k, {}).get("value", "")).strip()
    meta[slug] = {"title": title, "w": ii["width"], "h": ii["height"], "author": clean("Artist"), "license": clean("LicenseShortName"), "url": ii["descriptionurl"]}
    json.dump(meta, open(f"{out}/meta.json", "w"), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
    print(slug, len(data), meta[slug]["license"], meta[slug]["author"], flush=True)
    time.sleep(25)
EOF

content.content:
1:// Pin-jointed space truss, linear elastic. Pure: no DOM, no three.js. Units: mm, N.
7:// t = { nodes: [[x, y, z]], members: [{ ends: [i, j], EA }], fixed: [{ node, dof: "xyz" }], loads: [{ node, f: [fx, fy, fz] }] }.
8:// Returns node displacements u (mm) and member forces (N, + = tension). Supports must remove every rigid-body motion.
37:// Tubular frame from cross-sections. Each station { x, w (half width), z: [floor, sill, top] } has six nodes (left/right ×
38:// three levels), braced into a rigid ring. Each bay between stations: longitudinals, a diagonal in every side panel and in
39:// the floor, and optionally in the top. door: "high" keeps the full-height side truss (300 SL); "low" cuts it down to the
40:// sill, as a conventional door opening would (no top rail, no upper side diagonal); a station between two such bays
41:// then has no top ring either. node(s, side, level): side 0 = left (+y), 1 = right (−y); level 0 floor, 1 sill, 2 top.
65:// Torsion test: rear station held, one front corner lifted by F (N); the other front corner rests on a support.
66:// Returns stiffness (N·m per degree of twist) and the solution for drawing.

lines: +// Mercedes-Benz 300 (W 186) “Adenauer”, 1951–1957. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle centre on the
+// ground. Wheelbase, tracks and tyre size from the data sheet; corner masses, spring rates and the levelling motor's rate
+  title: "Level at the touch of a switch",
+  summary: "Germany's post-war flagship, the “Adenauer”, whose rear suspension could be stiffened up for a full load by an electric motor.",

+  lede: "Load a car with passengers and luggage and its rear sinks. The 300 has an extra torsion bar across its rear axle, and an electric motor can wind it up until the car sits level again. Load it and watch the rear come back up.",
+      { torus: { R: 275, r: 85, pos: [0, 740, 360], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                         // wheels
+        label: "Loading the car", level: "torsion", motorRate: 300,                          // motor rate illustrative
+        corners: { front: { mass: 460, extra: 40 }, rear: { mass: 410, extra: 140 } },         // illustrative
+        air: { area: 0.012, volume: 0.003, n: 1.3 },                                            // unused here (no bellows)
+        "Konrad Adenauer, West Germany's first chancellor, was driven in a series of these 300s, which gave the car its nickname. It was the largest and fastest German production car of its day.",
+        "At the rear sits a swing axle on coil springs. With a full load the rear sinks, the headlamps point up, and the rear wheels lean in.",

+        "An extra torsion bar runs across the rear axle. At the touch of a switch on the dashboard, an electric motor twists it further, and the added preload lifts the rear back to its normal height. Here it is shown acting on its own until the car is level.",

+        "The bar carries the extra load but adds no stiffness, so the ride frequency still drops as the load grows. Air springs avoid that: pumped up for the load they also get stiffer (see the 300 SEL 6.3).",
+  note: "The levelling here is proportional and automatic; on the car the driver switched the motor on. Masses and spring rates are round figures.",
+    "Corner masses, spring rates and the motor's preload rate",
+    "Ghost-body outline (traced from the data-sheet sizes and the photo)",
+// Mercedes-Benz 770 “Grosser Mercedes” (W 07), 1930–1938, Cabriolet F of Kaiser Wilhelm II. Frame: mm, x forward, y left,
+// z up; origin = front axle centre on the ground. Bore and stroke from the data sheet; engine position, conrod, body
+// outline and the supercharger's gearing illustrative.
+  summary: "The 7.7-litre straight-eight of the largest Mercedes-Benz of its time: two spark plugs in every cylinder, and a supercharger on full throttle.",

+  lede: "Built for heads of state, the 770 had to run, whatever happened. Each of its eight cylinders has two spark plugs, fed by two separate ignition systems. Watch both spark as each cylinder fires; then floor the throttle to bring in the supercharger.",
+      { torus: { R: 330, r: 100, pos: [0, 780, 440], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                             // wheels
+        label: "7.7-litre straight-eight · two plugs per cylinder · firing order 1-6-2-5-8-3-7-4",
+        order: [1, 6, 2, 5, 8, 3, 7, 4], bore: 95, stroke: 135, rod: 280,               // rod illustrative

+        "The 770 was the largest Mercedes-Benz of its day, built in small numbers for heads of state, royalty and the very wealthy. This Cabriolet F was made for the former Kaiser Wilhelm II, then living in exile in the Netherlands.",
+        "Eight cylinders in a row, 95 mm across and 135 mm stroke: 7.7 litres. In a straight-eight, one cylinder fires every quarter turn, so the drive is smooth and even.",

+        "Each cylinder has two spark plugs. One set is fired by a magneto, the other by a battery and coil. Lit at two points, the mixture burns through in about half the time, and if either system fails, the engine keeps running on the other.",
+        blower: { ratio: 2.6, engageAt: 0.98, tauUp: 0.25, tauDown: 0.7, boostMax: 0.4, psAtmo: 150, psBoost: 200 },   // ratio, timing and boost illustrative

+        "Like the SSK's, the 770's Roots supercharger runs only when it is needed. Push the accelerator to the floor and a clutch couples it to the crankshaft; it then blows air into the carburettor under pressure.",
+        "More air per stroke means more fuel can burn: 150 hp without the blower, 200 hp with it. Ease off and the clutch lets it go again, saving the engine and the fuel.",
+  note: "Several 770s survive; the museum's is the Cabriolet F that belonged to Wilhelm II.",
+    "Engine position in the car and conrod length",
+    "Valve gear drawn as overhead valves with pushrods",
+    "Supercharger gearing, engagement and boost (the 150 and 200 hp are quoted)",
+// Mercedes-Benz 180 “Ponton” (W 120), 1953–1962. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle centre on the
+// ground. Wheelbase and body size from the data sheet; the shell is drawn as a truss of its main members at illustrative
+// positions (stations from the bumper to the tail), with an illustrative member stiffness.
+  summary: "The first Mercedes-Benz saloons with a self-supporting body: floor, pillars and roof welded into one shell that carries the loads.",

+  lede: "Older cars put a body on a separate frame. The Ponton's body is the frame: sills, pillars and roof are welded into one shell. Twist it, as a car does when one wheel rides up a kerb, and compare it with a shallow frame under a body that carries nothing.",
+      { torus: { R: 255, r: 80, pos: [0, 715, 340], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                         // wheels
+        bays: [{ top: true }, { door: "high", top: true }, { door: "high", top: true }, { door: "high", top: true }, { top: true }],
+        EA: 15750000, load: 3000, exaggerate: 8,                                       // member stiffness illustrative
+        modes: { high: "Unit body: sides and roof carry the load", low: "Shallow frame: the body carries nothing" },

+        "Until the early 1950s a Mercedes-Benz car was a body bolted onto a separate frame. The Ponton saloons of 1953 onwards have a self-supporting body: floor, sills, pillars and roof are welded into one shell that carries the loads itself.",

+        "Twist it, as when one front wheel rides over a kerb: in a shell every panel and pillar takes part, so it barely deforms. A shallow frame under a body that carries nothing twists several times as far.",
+        "The shell is drawn here as a truss of its main members, coloured by force; the bending is hugely exaggerated.",
+        "“Ponton” (pontoon) describes the smooth, slab-sided body that takes in the wings instead of letting them stand out. The unit body also saved weight and made more room inside.",
+  note: "The research notes name the 220 of 1954; the photo shows a 1955 180, the first Ponton model.",
+    "Which Ponton is on show (the photo is a 1955 180; the research notes name the 220)",
+    "Ghost-body outline (traced from the data-sheet sizes and the photo)",

lines: +// Daimler motor carriage, 1886. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = REAR axle centre on the ground (the steering
+// subsystem's frame). Bore and stroke from the museum's figures; wheelbase, tracks, wheel sizes, engine position and conrod
+  summary: "The first four-wheeled motor car: a horse carriage that Gottlieb Daimler bought and fitted with his 1.1 hp engine.",

+  lede: "Gottlieb Daimler ordered an ordinary horse-drawn carriage and put his fast-running single-cylinder engine in it. The carriage kept its turntable front axle, which swings as a whole to steer. Watch the engine run, then the front axle turn.",
+        label: "Four-stroke cycle · one cylinder, hot-tube ignition",
+        order: [1], bore: 70, stroke: 120, rod: 300,                                // rod illustrative

+        "The engine is a development of Daimler and Maybach's “grandfather clock”: one upright cylinder of 462 cc, giving 1.1 hp at 650 rpm. It stands in the floor between the seats and drives the rear wheels through belts and gears.",
+        "There is no spark: a platinum tube, kept glowing by a burner, reaches into the cylinder. Compression pushes the mixture into the hot tube and it ignites.",
+        "The inlet valve is pulled open by the suction of the descending piston; a cam opens the exhaust valve.",
+        label: "Front steering, seen from above", start: "cp",
+        kingpinHalf: 560, arm: 150, wheelbase: 1700, stub: 60, frontR: 430, rearR: 560, halfTrackRear: 640, maxSteer: 30,   // illustrative
+        "Like any horse carriage, it steers with a turntable: the whole front axle swings about a pin at its middle, here moved by a tiller instead of the shafts of a horse.",
+        "It works, but the axle has to swing out of the way of the body, the car gets narrower on lock, and a bump on one wheel kicks the whole axle.",
+        "Compare the double pivot Karl Benz patented for his Victoria in 1893: each wheel turns on its own kingpin and the axle stays put.",
+  note: "Daimler's car of 1886 and Benz's Patent-Motorwagen were built a hundred kilometres apart, at the same time, by men who never met.",
+    "Engine position in the carriage and conrod length",
+// Mercedes-Simplex 60 PS touring limousine, 1904. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle centre on the
+// ground. Bore and stroke from the data sheet; engine position, conrod, cylinder spacing and body outline illustrative.
+  summary: "The 9.2-litre, 60 hp Simplex: overhead inlet valves opened by the camshaft, and well over 100 km/h.",

+  lede: "Each of its four cylinders is 140 mm across: together over nine litres. The 60 PS opens its inlet valves from the camshaft, through pushrods, instead of letting the suction pull them open. Watch the four cylinders fire in turn, slowed right down.",
+      { torus: { R: 400, r: 70, pos: [0, 700, 470], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                               // wheels
+        label: "9.2-litre four · overhead inlet valves · firing order 1-3-4-2",
+        order: [1, 3, 4, 2], bore: 140, stroke: 150, rod: 320,                    // rod illustrative
+        "Four cylinders of 140 mm bore and 150 mm stroke: 9.2 litres, giving 60 hp at little more than 1,000 rpm. With its light body the racing version reached over 100 km/h.",

+        "Earlier engines let the inlet valve open by suction, held shut only by a weak spring. The 60 PS opens it from the camshaft, through a pushrod and rocker, so the cylinder fills properly at speed.",
+        "It kept the layout of the first Mercedes of 1900: engine at the front under a low bonnet, honeycomb radiator, pressed-steel frame and a gate gearbox, a pattern cars kept for decades.",
+        "This one carries a tall touring-limousine body: room to stand up inside, for travelling in comfort.",
+  note: "The Simplex name stood for simple driving: the 1902 range was meant to be easy to handle compared with its predecessors.",
+    "Engine position in the car, cylinder spacing and conrod length",
+    "Valve gear drawn as overhead valves for both (the 60 PS had overhead inlet and side exhaust valves)",
+// Mercedes-Benz W 25 Grand Prix car, 1934. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle centre on the ground.
+// Bore and stroke from the data sheet; engine position, conrod and body outline illustrative.
+  summary: "The Grand Prix car built to a 750 kg weight limit, with a supercharged 3.4-litre straight-eight and two camshafts over its valves.",

+  lede: "The 1934 Grand Prix rules set no limit on the engine, only on the weight: 750 kg without driver, fuel, oil, water and tyres. So the W 25 got a light, fast-revving straight-eight with two overhead camshafts. Watch the cams open the valves as the eight cylinders fire in turn.",
+      { torus: { R: 330, r: 95, pos: [0, 680, 420], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                                                 // wheels
+        label: "M 25 supercharged straight-eight, twin overhead camshafts · firing order 1-6-2-5-8-3-7-4",
+        order: [1, 6, 2, 5, 8, 3, 7, 4], bore: 78, stroke: 88, rod: 180,                       // rod illustrative

+        "For 1934 the Grand Prix rules capped the car's weight at 750 kg, without driver, fuel, oil, water or tyres, in the hope of keeping speeds down. Mercedes-Benz answered with the W 25: about 350 hp from 3.4 litres.",

+        "Eight cylinders, 78 mm across with an 88 mm stroke. Two camshafts in the head, one for the inlet and one for the exhaust valves, open them directly, which lets the engine rev to almost 6,000 rpm.",
+        "A Roots supercharger blows air into the carburettors under pressure, so more fuel burns on every stroke.",

+        "The story goes that at the Eifel race of 1934 the car weighed a kilogram too much, so the white paint was scraped off overnight, leaving bare aluminium: the first Silver Arrow. Historians still argue about it.",
+  note: "The W 25 raced from 1934 to 1936; the museum shows it in its unpainted aluminium.",

lines: -  note: "Daimler's car of 1886 and Benz's Patent-Motorwagen were built a hundred kilometres apart, at the same time, by men who never met.",
+  note: "Daimler's car and Benz's Patent-Motorwagen were built in the same year, about a hundred kilometres apart, by two inventors working independently.",
"Engine position in the carriage and conrod length",
+// Mercedes-Benz LO 1112 bus, 1969, a Buenos Aires “colectivo”. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle
+// centre on the ground. Bore, stroke and firing order of the OM 352 from its data; engine position, conrod, compression
+  summary: "A brightly painted Buenos Aires colectivo on a short-bonnet lorry chassis, with a direct-injection six-cylinder diesel.",

+  lede: "Under the short bonnet of this Argentine bus runs the OM 352, one of Mercedes-Benz's first direct-injection diesels: the fuel is sprayed straight into a bowl in the piston, with no prechamber. Watch the injection come just before the top of each compression stroke.",
+      { torus: { R: 400, r: 110, pos: [0, 960, 480], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                                 // wheels
+        label: "OM 352 six-cylinder diesel, direct injection · firing order 1-5-3-6-2-4",
+        order: [1, 5, 3, 6, 2, 4], bore: 97, stroke: 128, rod: 230,                          // rod illustrative

+        "The LO 1112 is a lorry chassis with a short bonnet, bodied as a bus: in Argentina such buses, the colectivos, were built and painted by local coachbuilders and carried much of Buenos Aires' traffic.",
+        "Its engine, the OM 352, has six cylinders of 97 mm bore and 128 mm stroke: 5.7 litres. It was among the first Mercedes-Benz diesels to inject directly into the cylinder.",

+        "In a prechamber diesel such as the 260 D's, the fuel burns first in a small chamber in the head. Direct injection sprays it straight into a bowl in the piston crown: less heat is lost to the walls, so it uses less fuel and starts more easily.",
+        "Compressing the air alone heats it enough to light the fuel. There is no spark plug at all.",
+  note: "Mercedes-Benz built buses and lorries in Argentina from the early 1950s; many colectivos ran on its chassis.",
+    "Engine position, conrod length and compression ratio",
+    "Power figure (about 120 hp, from the model name)",
+// Mercedes-Benz LP 333, 1958–1961, the “millipede”. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = FIRST front axle centre
+// on the ground. Axle spacings, tracks, wheel size and steering arm geometry illustrative.
+  summary: "A cab-over lorry with two steered front axles, built to spread its load under new German axle-load limits.",

+  lede: "New rules in 1958 limited how much each axle of a lorry could carry. Mercedes-Benz's answer: a second steered axle at the front. For the tyres not to scrub, the second axle must steer less than the first. Turn the wheel and watch every wheel's axis meet at one point.",
+        kingpinHalf: 900, arm: 250, halfTrack: 1000, wheelR: 520, rearHalfTrack: 900, maxSteer: 35,   // illustrative

+        "German rules of the late 1950s cut the load each axle of a lorry could carry. To keep the payload, the LP 333 put two steered axles under its cab: three axles in all, which earned it the nickname “Tausendfüßler”, millipede.",

+        "For the tyres to roll without scrubbing, every wheel's axis must point to the same turning centre on the line of the rear axle. The second axle is closer to that line, so its wheels must turn less.",

+        "A drag link between the two axles' steering arms is proportioned to turn the second axle by just the right lesser angle. Each axle is also a double-pivot trapezoid, so its inner wheel turns more than its outer one.",
+        "Fix the second axle straight and its tyres are dragged sideways through every turn, wearing them and fighting the steering.",
+  note: "Shown from above with idealised trapezoids; the drag link is drawn between the left steering arms.",
+    "Axle spacings, tracks, wheel size and steering arm geometry",
+// Mercedes-Benz O 302 coach, 1974, the West German team bus of the 1974 World Cup. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up;
+// origin = front axle centre on the ground. Body size approximate; the heat-balance figures (thermal capacity, heat loss,
+  summary: "The coach that carried West Germany's footballers at the 1974 World Cup, with air conditioning on its roof.",

+  lede: "A coach in summer is a glasshouse full of people: each passenger gives off about as much heat as a light bulb, and the sun pours in through the windows. The unit on the roof takes that heat out. Fill the coach, switch the unit off and watch the temperature climb.",
+        label: "A full coach on a summer day",
+        cabin: { capacity: 400000, ua: 600, sun: 6000, person: 100, cooling: 20000, set: 24 },   // illustrative
+        passengers: { min: 0, max: 44, value: 30 }, outside: { min: 15, max: 35, value: 28 },

+        "Each passenger gives off about 100 watts of heat; forty of them add four kilowatts. Through the large windows the sun can add as much again, and on a warm day the outside air brings in more.",

+        "With no way to get rid of it, the saloon settles far above the outside temperature. Air conditioning removes the heat: refrigerant evaporating in the roof unit cools the air that fans blow down the length of the coach.",
+        "A thermostat holds the setting. Fill the coach on a hot day and the unit may reach its limit; the temperature then rises until the heat flowing out through the body balances the rest.",
+        "The O 302 was built from 1965 to the mid-1970s. This one took the West German team, the later world champions, to their matches in 1974.",
+  note: "One lump of air and interior with a single heat-loss figure: a heat balance to show the idea, not measurements of this coach.",
+    "Thermal capacity, heat loss, solar gain and cooling capacity",
+    "Whether this coach's unit is original equipment",

lines: +// Mercedes-Benz 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II, DTM racing car, 1992 (Klaus Ludwig). Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up;
+// origin = front axle centre on the ground. Drag coefficients, power and top speeds are those quoted for the road cars;
+// frontal areas, masses, rolling resistance and driveline efficiency illustrative.
+  summary: "The DTM homologation special whose wings and spoilers, shaped in the wind tunnel, gave it less drag than the plain 2.3-16.",

+  lede: "Its huge rear wing looks as if it must slow the car down. Wind-tunnel work on the whole body kit did the opposite: less drag than the earlier 2.3-16, and less lift too. Run both flat out and watch where engine power meets drag.",
+      { torus: { R: 255, r: 80, pos: [0, 745, 320], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                                         // wheels
+          { id: "evo2", label: "Evolution II body kit", cd: 0.29, area: 2.05, mass: 1420, crr: 0.013, eta: 0.82, ps: 235, quoted: 250 },   // area, mass, crr, eta illustrative
+          { id: "base", label: "2.3-16 body", cd: 0.32, area: 1.95, mass: 1380, crr: 0.013, eta: 0.82, ps: 185, quoted: 230 },
+        "Touring-car racing rules required a road version of every racing car: 502 Evolution IIs were built in 1990 so that the DTM car could race with its body kit.",

+        "The front spoiler, wide wheel arches, sill panels and adjustable rear wing were shaped in the wind tunnel as one system. The result: a drag coefficient of about 0.29 against the 2.3-16's 0.32, and much less lift at speed.",
+        "The power needed to push through the air grows with the cube of the speed. With 235 hp the road car reaches about 250 km/h.",
+        "This is Klaus Ludwig's DTM car of 1992; the race version had well over 350 hp. Its rear wing adds downforce at the cost of drag.",
+  note: "The aerodynamic figures here are the road cars'; the racing car in the museum was set up for downforce.",
+    "Frontal areas, masses, rolling resistance and driveline efficiency",
+    { label: "Wikipedia: Mercedes-Benz 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II", url: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_190_E_2.5-16_Evolution_II" },
+// Mercedes-Benz 300 GD (W 460) “Otto”, Gunther Holtorf's round-the-world G-Class. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up;
+// origin = front axle centre on the ground. Wheelbase and track from the data sheet; wheel loads, drive force, the slope's
+// resistance and the grip figures illustrative.
+  summary: "The G-Class that Gunther Holtorf drove for 26 years around the world: four-wheel drive engaged by hand, and differential locks front and rear.",

+  lede: "An open differential always sends the same torque to both sides, so one wheel on ice limits its partner. The G-Class can lock its axles together and then lock each differential. Put two wheels on ice and add one lock at a time until the car climbs.",
+      { torus: { R: 285, r: 95, pos: [0, 715, 380], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                              // wheels
+      id: "drive", label: "Four-wheel drive and locks", subsystem: "four-wheel-drive",
+        label: "Climbing a slope, seen from above",
+          { id: "one", label: "One rear wheel on ice", mu: [0.8, 0.8, 0.1, 0.8] },
+          { id: "diagonal", label: "Ice under two diagonal wheels", mu: [0.1, 0.8, 0.8, 0.1] },
+          { id: "three", label: "Three wheels on ice", mu: [0.1, 0.8, 0.1, 0.1] },
+          { id: "awd", label: "Four-wheel drive engaged", centre: true },
+          { id: "rear", label: "+ rear lock", centre: true, rear: true },
+          { id: "all", label: "+ front lock", centre: true, rear: true, front: true },
+        "An open differential lets the wheels on an axle turn at different speeds in a corner, but it always splits the torque equally. The wheel with the least grip sets the limit for both.",

+        "On this W 460 the driver engages the front axle by hand. That joins the front and rear propeller shafts rigidly, like a locked centre differential: an axle with a wheel on ice can no longer rob the other.",

+        "Then each axle's differential can be locked, rear first, then front: a locked axle turns as one shaft, and each wheel pushes as hard as its own grip allows. With all locks in, one wheel on dry ground can still move the car.",

+        "Gunther Holtorf drove this 300 GD, “Otto”, through Africa, Asia and the Americas from 1989 to 2014, nearly 900,000 km. Later G-Classes (W 463, from 1990) have permanent four-wheel drive with three locking differentials.",
+  note: "Locked axles are hard to steer and wear their tyres on firm ground: the locks are for loose or slippery ground only.",
+    "Wheel loads, drive force, slope resistance and grip figures",
+    "Whether Otto is on display (the photo is from the 2019–20 exhibition “40 years of the G-Class”)",
+// Mercedes-Benz ML 320 (W 163), 1997, the “Jurassic Park” car. Frame: mm, x forward, y left, z up; origin = front axle
+// centre on the ground. Wheelbase and track from the data sheet; wheel loads, drive force, brake force, slope resistance
+  summary: "The first M-Class, which made its debut in a dinosaur film: permanent four-wheel drive whose brakes stop a wheel from spinning.",

+  lede: "The M-Class has three open differentials and no locks. When a wheel starts to spin, its brake grips it, and the differential passes the torque across to the wheel that still has grip. Put wheels on ice and switch the system on.",
+      { torus: { R: 280, r: 95, pos: [0, 782, 370], rot: [90, 0, 0] }, mirror: true },                             // wheels
+        label: "Climbing a slope, seen from above",
+          { id: "one", label: "One rear wheel on ice", mu: [0.8, 0.8, 0.1, 0.8] },
+          { id: "diagonal", label: "Ice under two diagonal wheels", mu: [0.1, 0.8, 0.8, 0.1] },
+          { id: "three", label: "Three wheels on ice", mu: [0.1, 0.8, 0.1, 0.1] },
+          { id: "ets", label: "4ETS: brakes the spinning wheel", brake: 2500 },               // brake force illustrative
